Key ideas

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits

Definitions

Parallel circuit: a circuit that contains junctions; the current drawn from the battery, cell or electricity supply splits before it reaches components and rejoins afterwards

5D

New knowledgeParallel circuits: current, potential difference and resistance

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits

In a parallel circuit the path of the current branches so there is more than one way for current to go around the circuit.

This is different from the series circuits you have looked at so far (in Section 5C).

This means that in a parallel circuit, two or more components are connected across the same potential difference (A voltmeter is always connected in parallel, but it is built with a very high resistance so that negligible current travels through it.) Parallel circuits can be drawn in several ways (Figure 5D–1).

No matter which diagram is used, the effect is the same.

Figure 5D–1 Each of these diagrams show the same connections. The current leaving the supply splits into three, according to the size of the resistance in each branch, then rejoins the main circuit and returns through the battery. Each resistance has the same potential difference, the same as Vsupply.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 594
5D

New knowledgeParallel circuits: current, potential difference and resistance

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits

Each of the resistors is connected directly to a battery terminal, so each resistor receives the full potential difference supplied, Vsupply.

This is one major advantage of a parallel circuit over a series circuit.

Another is the ability to control each branch with a separate switch.

In parallel, each component can be switched on and off without affecting the others.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 595
5D

New knowledgeParallel circuits: current, potential difference and resistance

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits

Note that for parallel circuits, the: • same potential difference, V, is across each component in the parallel section • current, Itotal, must divide into three component currents, I1, I2 and I3.

It must therefore be true that Itotal = I1 + I2 + I3.

Starting with Iequivalent = I1 + I2 + I3 and substituting for I from V Ohm’s law, I = , for each branch of the circuit gives: R V V V V supply supply supply supply = + + R R R R equivalent 1 2 3 Taking Vsupply as a common factor on the right-hand side and cancelling gives: 1 1 1 1 = + + R R R R equivalent 1 2 3 The general form of this formula, for any number of resistors in parallel, is: If there are only two resistors, the parallel equivalent resistance formula reduces to: Formula 5D–2 is generally easier to apply than Formula 5D–1.

It also works for three or more resistors, by applying it first to two, then applying the formula again using that equivalent resistance with the next resistor, and so on.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 596
5D

New knowledgeParallel circuits: current, potential difference and resistance

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits

In general, the equivalent resistance calculated in either parallel or series (or combined) gives the value of a single resistor that could replace a number of individual resistors, to give the same effect in the circuit.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 597

New knowledgeA graphical method for series and parallel circuits

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits

So far two formulas have been used to calculate the equivalent resistance of simple circuits.

For series combinations: For parallel circuits: 1 1 1 1 = + + Requivalent = R1 + R2 + … Rn R R R R equivalent 1 2 3 When designing circuits with several components, their total resistance must be found before the circuit can be fully analysed.

Components may be connected in series, in parallel or in a combination of the two.

A graphical method allows you to predict the way a circuit will behave from the characteristics of the individual components.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 648

New knowledgeResistors in series: a graphical method

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits

The components in the circuit shown in Figure 5D–2 have resistances of 2 Ω and 3 Ω respectively.

A characteristic graph of I vs V can be created for each component separately, using the techniques learned in Section 5C.

Then you can use the graph to analyse the circuit as follows.

As it’s a series circuit, the current is the same through each resistor.

Figure 5D–2 A graphical method for calculating the total resistance in a series circuit (top). As the current flowing through each component must be the same, the individual potential drops across each component can easily read off the graph. A graph of I–V (bottom) can be constructed for the series combination (black dotted line).
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 6510
5D

New knowledgeResistors in series: a graphical method

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits

Choosing a current of 2 A, for example, the p.d. across each component is read from the graph (4 V and 6 V).

The total p.d. is the sum of these two values, so a point can be plotted on the graph corresponding to the V I ratio for the total resistance (10 V, 2 A).

An I vs V graph for the combination of resistors is plotted point by point for each current value (dotted line).

The total resistance is V the value of I determined from this graph, 5 Ω in this case.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 6511

New knowledgeResistors in series: a graphical method

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits

This is the sum of 2 Ω and 3 Ω, as you would expect from Requivalent = R1 + R2 + … Rn.

This constructed graph can be compared to the results measured from current through and potential difference across the whole combination.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 6512
5D

New knowledgeResistors in parallel: a graphical method

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits

For a parallel combination, using the same I–V characteristic graph of the individual components, the analysis is as follows.

As it’s a parallel circuit (Figure 5D–3), the potential difference across each resistor is the same.

Choosing a potential difference (6 V for example), the current through each resistance is read from the graph (2 A and 3 A).

The total current in the circuit is then the sum of the two separate currents (5 A).

Figure 5D–3 A simple graphical method for calculating the total resistance in the parallel circuit on the left. As the voltage across each element must be the same, the individual current flowing through each component can be easily read off the graph on the right.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 6513
5D

New knowledgeResistors in parallel: a graphical method

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits

A point can be plotted corresponding to the values of V and I for the equivalent resistance of the circuit (6 V, 5 A).

An I vs V graph can be plotted point by point for each value of p.d. (for the combination of resistors).

Again, the ratio V I from the inverse gradient of this graph is equal to the total resistance, 6 1 1 1 1 5 = 1.25 Ω in this case, as you would expect from the formula . = 1 1 R R R Rn equivalent 1 2 Notice that the I–V graph for series resistors has a smaller gradient, meaning Requivalent is larger than either component; the I–V graph for parallel resistors has a steeper gradient, meaning smaller resistance than either component.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 6514

Working

=127= \frac{12}{7}=712​
=1.71 Ω= 1.71\ \Omega=1.71 Ω

=4+312= \frac{4+3}{12}=124+3​
=712= \frac{7}{12}=127​

1Requivalent=110+115+125\frac{1}{R_{\text{equivalent}}} = \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{25}Requivalent​1​=101​+151​+251​

Working

First notice that the top branch of the circuit consists of two resistors in series. Therefore, the equivalent resistance of the top branch is given by:
Rtop=R1+R2=(4)+(4)=8 ΩR_{\text{top}} = R_1 + R_2 = (4) + (4) = 8\ \OmegaRtop​=R1​+R2​=(4)+(4)=8 Ω

Now you can apply the formula for two resistances in parallel:
Requivalent=R1R2R1+R2R_{\text{equivalent}} = \frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2}Requivalent​=R1​+R2​R1​R2​​
=(8)(2)(8)+(2)= \frac{(8)(2)}{(8)+(2)}=(8)+(2)(8)(2)​
=1610= \frac{16}{10}=1016​
=1.6 Ω= 1.6\ \Omega=1.6 Ω
Therefore, the equivalent resistance is 1.6 Ω.
Alternatively: 1Requivalent=1R1+1R2\frac{1}{R_{\text{equivalent}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}Requivalent​1​=R1​1​+R2​1​
Therefore: 1Requivalent=18+12\frac{1}{R_{\text{equivalent}}} = \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{2}Requivalent​1​=81​+21​
=1+48= \frac{1+4}{8}=81+4​
=58= \frac{5}{8}=85​
Requivalent=85=1.6 ΩR_{\text{equivalent}} = \frac{8}{5} = 1.6\ \OmegaRequivalent​=58​=1.6 Ω
The equivalent resistance is 1.6 Ω, as expected.

We doGraphical approach to series resistance

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits
A 3 Ω and 4 Ω resistor are wired in series. Use a graphical approach to determine the total potential difference across each resistor if the current is 2 A. Hence find the equivalent resistance of the series combination.
Key idea · Formula 5D–1 Parallel resistance1Requivalent=1R1+1R2+⋯+1Rn\frac{1}{R_{\text{equivalent}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \dots + \frac{1}{R_n}Requivalent​1​=R1​1​+R2​1​+⋯+Rn​1​

Working

The III–VVV curve of a 3 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor are shown. (see image)
Reading off the graph for a current of 2 A, the resistance of 3 Ω contributes 6 V of potential difference, and the resistance of 4 Ω contributes 8 V of potential difference.
Therefore, the total potential difference across the resistances is 6 + 8 = 14 V.
Requivalent=VtotalIR_{\text{equivalent}} = \frac{V_{\text{total}}}{I}Requivalent​=IVtotal​​
=142= \frac{14}{2}=214​
=7 Ω= 7\ \Omega=7 Ω
This is what you would expect from the formula.
14 V; 7 Ω
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 66, Worked example 5D-320

The III–VVV curve of a 3 Ω and 4 Ω resistor are shown above. (see image)

So, the total current through the battery is 4 + 3 = 7 A.
To find RequivalentR_{\text{equivalent}}Requivalent​:
Requivalent=VIequivalentR_{\text{equivalent}} = \frac{V}{I_{\text{equivalent}}}Requivalent​=Iequivalent​V​
=127= \frac{12}{7}=712​
=1.7 Ω= 1.7\ \Omega=1.7 Ω
You can check the answer for this simple case using the formula for parallel resistance (Formula 5D–1 or 5D–2).
7 A; 1.7 Ω

Explain, using two equations, why resistance increases in a series circuit as more resistors are added but decreases in a parallel circuit when more resistors are added.

Working

In a series circuit, equivalent resistance is the sum of all the resistances: Requivalent=R1+R2+R3+…R_{\text{equivalent}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \dotsRequivalent​=R1​+R2​+R3​+… Therefore, resistance increases with more resistors added. (1 mark) In a parallel circuit, the equivalent resistance is calculated by: 1Requivalent=1R1+1R2+1R3+…\frac{1}{R_{\text{equivalent}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3} + \dotsRequivalent​1​=R1​1​+R2​1​+R3​1​+… Therefore, resistance decreases as more resistors are added. (1 mark)

You trySection 5D questions Q13

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits
Series and parallel circuits have different advantages (and disadvantages). Which type of circuit would be better for each of the following uses. Sketch a circuit diagram for each. a A circuit with a heating coil and a warning light, for an electric kettle. The light must show when the coil is heating. b A circuit with two lights and one switch, where each light needs to be as bright as the other and receive the full potential difference. c A battery backup safety circuit with two switches and one light, for the top and bottom of a stairwell. See if you can design this one!

Working

a Series circuit works best. Warning light needs to accommodate a high current, but will only use a small amount of the potential difference. b Parallel circuit works best, with the switch beside the battery so it controls both globes at once. c Several possibilities, including: (see answer image) This requires a special type of switch: 'double pole, single throw' at each end of the stairwell. If either switch is changed from its starting position, it will change the state of the light: off-to-on or vice versa.

Modelling resistance in parallel circuits
Check-in set 2 · Q1 · 5D
Explain why you read off potential differences at a fixed current in the graphical approach for resistances in series.
In a series circuit, there is only one path electrons can flow. This means that the current is the same at all points in the circuit, and the quantity that changes around the circuit is the potential difference.
Check-in set 2 · Q2 · 5D
Explain why you read off currents at a fixed potential difference in the graphical approach for resistances in parallel.
In a parallel circuit, all resistors are subjected to the same potential difference produced by the power source. This means that the quantity that changes around the circuit is the current.
